newsitem.title: USA: Market timers spur US junk bond sales, not stampede.
newsitem.headline: Market timers spur US junk bond sales, not stampede.

text.p: Cash outflows from high-yield mutual funds by "market timer" money managers have fueled a recent drop in prices, junk bond players said this week.
At the same time, however, most of those players remained upbeat for the longer term amid an economy that is expanding and that is, as of yet, undisturbed by inflation.

George Edwards, a portfolio manager with Prudential Investments, said market timers have contributed to a seepage of cash out of his funds and that he would not be surprised to see very small inflows or a negative read from widely-watched AMG Data Services on Friday morning.
With that said, however, Edwards noted there was no overwhelming retreat from high-yield, calling the back-up a modest correction.
AMG Data reported "healthy" inflows of $526 million in the week ended February 26, market sources said.

"We haven't seen any stampede out and we haven't seen bid lists," Edwards said. "There are a couple of guys you typically see trying to raise cash in fairly good size when the timers move big time. So far we haven't seen that."
But other street sources insisted the Zurich Kemper Mutual Funds, which are said to manage a large amount of "market timer" money, has been selling high-yield bonds.
Harry Resis, co-manager of roughly $4.5 billion in high-yield assets at Kemper, was unavailable for comment.

"Market timers" are professional money managers who invest in a portfolio of mutual funds, mostly for institutional clients. They are known for making quick investment decisions, moving significant sums into and out of different funds based on small changes in the market.
Managers interviewed were of similar minds in that they all expected the price weakness to be temporary.

"This will be a short-term impact -- two weeks at the most," said Mark Durbiano, who manages $2.9 billion in high-yield bonds for Federated Investors. "(Market timer) moves tend to be very quick and very concentrated -- as soon as selling pressure lessens, all that money will come back."

Thomas Ole Dial, executive vice president and chief investment officer at The Northstar Funds, noted the market has come so far so fast that some selling should come as no surprise. What is soothing, he said, is that he does not see selling as a result of investor redemptions.
In fact, Dial said it is far from a buyer's market because a good bond is still hard to find -- not as challenging as one week ago, he acknowledged, but hard.

"I see a lot of selling between dealers that were long," Dial said. "But...we're sitting with a couple of hundred million dollars in cash trying to buy bonds and I'm having trouble getting good offerings."
And because the market is undeniably and perhaps unreasonably tight, comments delivered by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan last week gave investors reason to pause, Dial said.

In the first leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last week, Greenspan warned that financial markets, including stock and junk bond markets, may be overly optimistic about the economy and urged caution.

"Greenspan was saying spreads are too tight on high-yield bonds and there should be wider spreads to compensate for the risks you're taking," Dial said. "If anything, it's people reevaluating where some of these things should trade.
Amid the skittish tone, Prudential's Edwards said some accounts have been capitalizing on what they believed to be the most vulnerable sector with the most supply -- telecommunications.

"If you're going to play the market for a trade, you figure at the margin mutual fund money would get a little skittish here, you'd probably go after communications and try to set up a few shorts there in anticipation of buying them back a couple points cheaper on Friday."
High-yield deals slated for the near-term may well begin to disappear from the calendar, he opined.
((--U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1672))
